readings.title: The Bicyclopædia Bird, part 2: why the Pollywog is always amiable
readings.challenge: Find the word games hidden in answers that sound wise.
readings.focus: The Bicyclopædia Bird answers Jimmieboy’s questions with a poem about the Pollywog and some very strange explanations.
readings.context: John Kendrick Bangs wrote these funny stories about a small boy called Jimmieboy, who meets talking creatures that explain the world in their own upside-down way. Jimmieboy has met the Bicyclopædia Bird, a bird hidden in a bush who rides a bicycle and knows everything; its name joins “encyclopaedia,” a book of all knowledge, and “bicycle.” Because Jimmieboy did not laugh at its looks, it has promised to answer any question he asks. Amiable means good-natured; a pollywog is a tadpole; to assuage hunger is to ease it; an angle-worm is an earthworm; a virtue is a good quality; to discombobulate is to muddle someone up.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Bicyclopædia Bird,” from Jimmieboy’s first question through the poem “The Pollywog” to the use of weeds; opens “"That's very nice of you," returned Jimmieboy; "and perhaps, to begin with, you'll tell…”; closes “…out they make your lawns prettier. That's one of the simplest things in the world.”.

questions.prompt: How did the Pollywog lose his temper, and why has it never come back?
facilitatorNotes: He bit a rusty nail thinking it was a worm, hurt both jaws, and got so angry that his temper “simply went” and has never been found. The joke is that “losing your temper” usually means getting angry.
evidence: His temper simply went.
It has not since been found.

questions.prompt: The Bird says the sun rises “For the same reason that you do.” What is that reason? Is it a real answer?
facilitatorNotes: “Because it is time to get up.” It sounds like an answer, but it is a joke: it treats the sun like a sleepy boy.
evidence: Because it is time to get up.

questions.prompt: Why does Jimmieboy think “alarm-clock” is a bad name, and how does the Bird explain it?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmieboy says it never frightens anybody. The Bird says it frightens the creatures in your dreams, and the noise they make running away wakes you up, as when a catfish in the Bird’s dream fled at the ring.
evidence: it doesn't ever alarm anybody
It alarms the people or the animals you dream about when you are asleep

questions.prompt: The Bird says weeds make lawns prettier next year. How? Do you believe it?
facilitatorNotes: When you make the weeds get out, the lawn looks better. It is true in a back-to-front way. Children may enjoy spotting that the Bird’s answers are clever tricks rather than facts, and say which answer they liked best.
evidence: By getting out they make your lawns prettier.

readings.title: The Bicyclopædia Bird, part 3: the house with no shutters
readings.challenge: Notice how one word can mean two very different things.
readings.focus: The Bird tells of a mean man’s house blown away by cyclones, explains houses with wings, and then flees.
readings.context: Recap: Jimmieboy has met the Bicyclopædia Bird, a bird hidden in a bush who rides a bicycle and knows everything; its name joins “encyclopaedia,” a book of all knowledge, and “bicycle.” Because Jimmieboy did not laugh at its looks, it has promised to answer any question he asks. It has explained why the Pollywog is never cross, why an alarm-clock is called that, and what weeds are for. Shutters are wooden covers that close over windows; a cyclone is a whirling windstorm; foundations are the stones a house stands on; a wing of a house is a part built out to one side.
readings.contentNote: In the Bird’s tall tale a whole family of nineteen is carried off by cyclones and never comes down; Jimmieboy finds it dreadful to think about.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, from the Bird’s question about shutters to the end of the chapter; opens “But here's a thing I should think you'd wonder at. Why do houses have shutters on their…”; closes “…the air. He really felt as if he would like to try the experiment with his own house.”.

questions.prompt: Jimmieboy says shutters keep the sun out. What does the Bird say they are really for?
facilitatorNotes: To bang about on windy nights and wake people up. It says the sun is too big to get into a house anyway.
evidence: So as to wake people up by banging about on windy nights

questions.prompt: What happened to the Podlingtons, and whom does the Bird blame?
facilitatorNotes: Three cyclones blew their house up into the air ten years ago, and it has never come down. The Bird blames Mr. Podlington, who was rich but too mean to buy shutters.
evidence: Mr. Podlington was very rich, but awful mean
It was Mr. Podlington's meanness about the shutters, and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Jimmieboy’s house has three wings. What does he mean by “wings,” and what does the Bird mean?
facilitatorNotes: Jimmieboy means parts of the house, such as the new kitchen; the Bird means wings for flying. The joke is the two meanings of one word.
evidence: One of 'em was put on it last summer, so that we could have a bigger kitchen.
Wings are meant to fly with, aren't they?

questions.prompt: Why does the Bird run away just before it explains how to fly a house? Why might Bangs stop the answer there?
facilitatorNotes: The alarm-clock rings, and the Bird is terrified of alarms, perhaps because of its dream about the catfish. Bangs leaves the impossible question unanswered, so Jimmieboy, and we, are left wondering. Some children will say the Bird never knew the answer at all.
evidence: The alarm! The alarm!
wishing that the alarm-clock had held off just a little longer

readings.title: Giant the Jack Killer, part 1: the Giant’s complaint
readings.challenge: Imagine how a story looks from the inside, to the characters in it.
readings.focus: The Giant in Jimmieboy’s fairy book steps to his door and asks for help: he is tired of being killed by Jack every day.
readings.context: John Kendrick Bangs wrote these funny stories about a small boy called Jimmieboy, who meets talking creatures that explain the world in their own upside-down way. In the fairy tale “Jack the Giant Killer,” a brave boy named Jack kills one giant after another. An ogre is a man-eating giant; genial means friendly; a ruffian is a rough bully; a tragedy is a sad story; a breach of contract is breaking an agreement; “as lief” means as gladly.
readings.contentNote: The Giant talks cheerfully about killing and being killed; it is all pretend, and no one is hurt.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “Giant the Jack Killer,” from the picture of the castle to Jimmieboy’s going to find Jack; opens “Jimmieboy was turning over the pages of his fairy book the other night, trying to refresh…”; closes “…on the soles of the shoes of another giant, whom he had bound and strapped to the floor.”.

questions.prompt: What does Jimmieboy see happen in the picture of the Giant’s castle?
facilitatorNotes: The doorknob moves, the door opens, and the Giant puts his head out, winks and smiles.
evidence: the moving thing was the knob of the castle door

questions.prompt: What does the Giant want, and why does he think it is fair?
facilitatorNotes: To kill Jack just once, for a change, because being killed every day by someone so small is tiresome.
evidence: The idea of a big thing like me being killed every day of his life by a mosquito like Jack is very tiresome

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t the Giant stay dead when Jack kills him?
facilitatorNotes: Because he has to be ready to be killed again the next time someone reads the story, every day for three years in Jimmieboy’s case.
evidence: if we staid dead how do you suppose we'd be on hand to be killed again the next time you had the story read to you?

questions.prompt: The Giant calls Jack a ruffian but says, “all I am I owe to him.” How can both be true?
facilitatorNotes: Being killed by Jack is his job: in return he gets a free castle and the fairy people’s riches. So he has no hard feelings. Children can talk about what it would be like to be a character in a book read every night.
evidence: Why, all I am I owe to him.
So you see I haven't any hard feelings against him

readings.title: Giant the Jack Killer, part 2: the plum-pudding plan
readings.challenge: Follow a plan that is clever, kind and silly all at once.
readings.focus: Jack agrees to let the Giant win once a week, if he may choose how it is done.
readings.context: Recap: John Kendrick Bangs wrote these funny stories about a small boy called Jimmieboy, who meets talking creatures that explain the world in their own upside-down way. The Giant in Jimmieboy’s fairy book has asked him to persuade Jack the Giant Killer to let the Giant kill Jack just once a week, on Saturday nights, painlessly and only for pretend. Hop o’ My Thumb and Jack and the Beanstalk are other fairy tales; monotonous means dull because it is always the same; circumference is the distance round something.
readings.contentNote: Jack and Jimmieboy discuss, as a joke, ways of being killed and eaten.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, from Jimmieboy’s visit to Jack to the end of the chapter; opens “At first Jimmieboy did not know how to address him. He had often spoken to the figures in…”; closes “…turned up, so that I really cannot tell you whether or not the arrangement was a success.”.

questions.prompt: What does Jack think of the Giant?
facilitatorNotes: He calls him a good fellow who dies as easily as falling off a log; out of working hours they are great chums.
evidence: out of business hours we're great chums

questions.prompt: Why does Jack hope the Giant won’t leave his job?
facilitatorNotes: If the Giant went over to the Beanstalk story, he would have to fall a mile and be hurt; Jack’s way of killing him is painless.
evidence: You can't fall a mile without getting hurt, you know

questions.prompt: Explain Jack’s plum-pudding plan. How would he escape?
facilitatorNotes: He would be baked in the middle of a huge plum-pudding; the Giant would eat from the outside while Jack ate from the inside, and by the time the Giant reached him he would be too full.
evidence: while he is eating it from the outside I could be eating it from the inside

questions.prompt: Jack says the Giant “just wants to seem to win once.” Why might seeming to win be enough?
facilitatorNotes: The Giant does not want to hurt Jack; he wants a turn at being the winner. Children may think of games where everyone should get a chance to win.
evidence: He just wants to seem to win once.

questions.prompt: The chapter ends: “As yet that Saturday night has not turned up.” Why do you think Bangs doesn’t tell us how it went?
facilitatorNotes: Saturday is always coming but never quite here in the story; leaving it open lets us imagine the new ending ourselves. Some children may suspect the old ending will always win, because that is how the book is printed.
evidence: As yet that Saturday night has not turned up

readings.title: Jimmieboy and the Fireworks: the Dreadful Fate of Naughty Nate
readings.challenge: Notice how a storyteller pretends not to know things, and why that makes a poem funny.
readings.focus: On the night before the Fourth of July a talking Rocket recites the tale of a boy who disobeyed his father and flew off on a rocket, and then the fireworks start going off.
readings.context: John Kendrick Bangs wrote these funny stories about a small boy called Jimmieboy, who meets talking creatures that explain the world in their own upside-down way. On the evening of July 3rd, Jimmieboy has crept down to the room where the family’s fireworks are kept and found them alive, telling jokes and rehearsing for the next day. The Pin Wheel has asked the Rocket to recite his poem about Nate. To abide is to put up with; to gyrate is to whirl round; astronomers study the stars; a Roman candle shoots out balls of fire; a set piece is a frame of fireworks that spells out a picture or words.
readings.contentNote: In the poem a boy who disobeys his father is carried off by a rocket and never seen again. In Jimmieboy’s dream the fireworks catch fire and go off indoors.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IX, “Jimmieboy and the Fireworks,” from the Rocket’s offer to tell the story of Nate to the end of the chapter; opens “"Would you like to hear that story, Jimmieboy?" asked the Rocket.”; closes “…middle of the floor just where it had fallen. Which Jimmieboy thinks was very singular.”.

questions.prompt: The poem keeps saying it does not know things: the year, the place, the father’s job. Why might the poet pretend not to know?
facilitatorNotes: It is a joke: the poem sounds like a serious true tale but cannot remember anything that would make it true. Children may enjoy the silly guesses, such as the Governor of “Floridee.”
evidence: I don't recall the date
I really can't locate

questions.prompt: What is the one thing Nate’s father forbids? Why might that make Nate want it more?
facilitatorNotes: Sky-rockets. Nate can buy anything else, so the one forbidden thing becomes the one he wants. Ask whether children know that feeling.
evidence: Sky-rockets I cannot abide
But Nate, alas! did not obey

questions.prompt: Jimmieboy says the poem makes him unhappy. How does the Rocket comfort him?
facilitatorNotes: The best thing about the story is that it never happened; and if it did, Nate might come back in six or seven million years, though he would be late for tea. The Rocket answers worry with a joke.
evidence: the best thing about it is that it never happened
that would make him late for tea

questions.prompt: How does the dream end, and what clue suggests it might not all have been a dream?
facilitatorNotes: The set piece spells “Wake up, and go to bed right,” the very words his father is saying as Jimmieboy wakes on the lounge. Yet a broken torpedo lies on the floor just where one fell in the dream, which Jimmieboy thinks very singular. Children can decide.
evidence: Wake up, and go to bed right.
except the broken torpedo, which was found in the middle of the floor

readings.title: Jimmieboy’s Photograph: the Horrid Fate of Jumping Sam
readings.challenge: Decide whether a moral is meant seriously, and find the clues.
readings.focus: A blurred photograph, spoiled because Jimmieboy wiggled, tells of boys who would not stand still, ending with a poem about a boy who jumps around the world.
readings.context: John Kendrick Bangs wrote these funny stories about a small boy called Jimmieboy, who meets talking creatures that explain the world in their own upside-down way. Jimmieboy wriggled while his photograph was taken, so the first print came out blurred and was thrown aside; the rejected picture has begun to talk to him. Photographs then took several seconds to make, so sitters had to keep perfectly still. Perth is a city in Scotland and in Australia, and Allahabad a city in India; to abate is to lessen or stop; a visage is a face; mirth is merriment.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “Jimmieboy’s Photograph,” from the picture’s warning about “movey boys” to the end of the chapter; opens “"Boys don't know what a terrible lot of horrid things happen because they don't stand…”; closes “…perhaps the brief life and long poem of the rejected picture were not wasted after all.”.

questions.prompt: What does the picture mean by “movey boys”?
facilitatorNotes: Boys who do not stand still when they ought to, like Jimmieboy at the photographer’s. The picture blames them for “untold misery.”
evidence: boys that don't stand still when they ought to

questions.prompt: How could one boy shake a whole town to pieces? Follow the chain.
facilitatorNotes: His jumping shook the nursery, the nursery shook the house, the house the lot, the lot the street, and the street the town. Then everyone moved away and took the town’s name, which is why the picture cannot say where it was: a joke inside a joke.
evidence: and the street shook the whole town
took the name of the town with them

questions.prompt: How do Sam’s jumps grow, and where is he going at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Two feet, then three, then a mile or two, twenty miles, across states and countries, around the earth, and at last to the moon. Each stanza makes the jump bigger.
evidence: He leaped two feet at first, they say, And then he made it three.
Was jumping to the moon

questions.prompt: The poem says its own moral is “shown with little skill.” Is the picture serious? Does it work on Jimmieboy?
facilitatorNotes: The poem laughs at itself, yet Jimmieboy keeps very still while he thinks, then starts wiggling again. The last paragraph says he has practised standing still since. Children can decide whether the lesson was serious, funny, or both.
evidence: Though shown with little skill
Jimmieboy has practiced standing still very often since the affair happened
